results.title: Data-driven analysis and forecasting of highway traffic dynamics
results.content: Here we demonstrate how the Koopman mode decomposition can offer a model-free, data-driven approach for analyzing and forecasting traffic dynamics. In this work, we demonstrate how the spectral properties of the Koopman operator, specifically the Koopman mode decomposition (KMD), can offer a model-free, parameter-free, data-driven approach for accurately identifying, analyzing and forecasting spatiotemporal traffic patterns. In this work, we have utilized the Hankel dynamic mode decomposition algorithm (Hankel-DMD)49,55 to approximate the Koopman modes and eigenvalues of traffic data. ### Koopman mode analysis of spatiotemporal traffic data We begin by studying the NGSIM data set collected by the US Federal Highway Administration. Koopman modes demonstrating our method’s ability to uncover patterns hidden within traffic velocity data. ### Koopman mode analysis of multi-lane traffic data We demonstrate how the KMD readily generalizes to the multi-lane scenario by analyzing multi-lane spatiotemporal density data for the US-101 highway. The historic and real-time nature of the PeMs repository has led to its widespread use for implementing and verifying forecasting methodologies5,36.We have developed a moving horizon Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (MH-HDMD) algorithm which utilizes a subset of _s_ data vectors (sampling window) to forecast the next _f_ data vectors (forecast window) updated every _h_ time steps (horizon window). ### Forecasting and analysis of multi-lane network traffic data In this section, we demonstrate how the KMD can be utilized to analyze and forecast highway traffic at the multi-lane network scale. We plot in Fig. 9a a map, taken from Map data ©2019 Google, of Los Angeles with the highways studied highlighted, a plot of the 24-hour Koopman modes (Fig.9b) along with the average phase and magnitude (Fig.9c, d). ### Koopman mode decomposition of highway traffic dynamics In this section, we outline the general theory and setting of the Koopman mode decomposition and its data-driven implementation to highway traffic data. We now discuss the details of how the Koopman mode decomposition can be applied to highway traffic data.

00:00 We are given two normal modes on a string clamped at both ends, and we are given the linear density of the string, which we immediately convert into the SI units of kg/m.

🧠 Access full flipped physics courses with video lectures and examples at https://www.zakslabphysics.com/

We are given the frequency of a normal mode with four antinodes, so this is the fourth harmonic.  In addition, we are given the frequency of a normal mode with five antinodes, so this is the fifth harmonic.

01:09 To find the fundamental frequency, we apply the equation f_n=nf_1 (in other words the frequency of each harmonic is an integer multiple of the fundamental or first harmonic).  We simply solve for f_1 to get f_1=f_n/n, and we calculate the first harmonic frequency for the string.  The second given normal mode (the fifth harmonic) allows us to double check our work with the same calculation, and the two answers agree.

02:06 Next, we compute the wave velocity on the string using the wave speed equation v=f*lambda.  We can pick either given normal mode for the calculation, and the only tricky part is figuring out the wavelength of each normal mode.  In the fourth harmonic, we see exactly two wavelengths on the string, so the wavelength is just half the length of the string.  We plug in the frequency of the fourth harmonic and the wavelength of the fourth harmonic and obtain the wave speed on the string.  Once again, we double check our work using the fifth hamonic.

03:47 Finally, we compute the tension in the string by using the equation v=sqrt(T/mu), we solve for T to get T=v^2*mu, plug in the known wave speed and linear density, and we've got the wave speed on the string.
